title: One Substrate No Longer Rules Them All
gist: Advanced-package substrates are becoming application-specific: larger, higher-layer, finer-routed AI substrates turn a capacity problem into a capability and yield problem, shrinking qualified supply and pushing specialization into temporary-bond materials, glass liners and equipment. No single successor (organic, glass, bridges) will win; AI, co-packaged optics and automotive pull substrate requirements in different directions.

themes.theme: Substrate: from capacity problem to capability problem

insights.claim: Advanced-package substrate constraints have shifted from a pure capacity shortage to a capability problem: a supplier can have open capacity yet be unable to build the larger, higher-layer, finer-routed substrates modern AI packages need.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Aggregate substrate capacity figures overstate usable supply for AI packages; capability-qualified vendors hold pricing power.
insights.quote: a supplier can have available capacity and still be unable to build the substrate needed for a modern advanced package

insights.claim: Substrate market value is growing faster than unit shipments because each package uses higher layer counts and larger body sizes, consuming more material per unit.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Substrate revenue can grow even with flat units; track value/ASP rather than volume for substrate makers.
insights.quote: Substrate value is rising faster than shipment volume because packages are using higher layer counts and larger body sizes

insights.claim: According to Prismark, servers remain the strongest substrate growth area, particularly large-body flip-chip BGA packages.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Server/AI demand is the key driver for high-end FC-BGA substrate suppliers.
insights.quote: The strongest growth area is still servers, particularly large-body flip-chip BGA packages.

insights.claim: Two organic substrate suppliers making the same package footprint are not necessarily interchangeable, since dielectric properties, line/space, layer stack, CTE, embedded passives, power delivery and thermal behavior narrow acceptable choices.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Supplier substitution risk is higher than footprint-level comparisons suggest.

insights.claim: The organic-vs-silicon-vs-glass debate is somewhat misleading because specialization is already happening within each substrate family, e.g. Shinko offers three core-layer structures and four-, six- and eight-layer cores and customers now ask for passives embedded in the core for power integrity.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Investors framing substrates as a glass-replaces-organic race may miss intra-organic differentiation opportunities.
insights.quote: Now customers are asking us to embed passive components in the core for power integrity.

themes.theme: Yield sets the real design rules

insights.claim: A substrate specification can be technically achievable but economically unattractive because more layers, larger bodies and tighter routing narrow several tolerances simultaneously until nominal capability no longer translates into production yield.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Yield, not lab capability, determines which substrate technologies ramp profitably.

insights.claim: Amkor says substrate suppliers push back on desired design rules for large-body multilayer structures because of yield hits, forcing the OSAT to adapt assembly choices among mass reflow, laser-assisted bonding or thermocompression bonding.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Assembly-process mix (e.g., TCB adoption) is being driven by substrate yield limits.
insights.quote: if we do that, it will hit their yield because these are large-body, multilayer structures
insights.locator: We may want certain design rules

insights.claim: Process windows are no longer reusable across customers: Amkor says each customer requires development work before verification and high-volume manufacturing, so an established window is a starting point rather than an answer.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Rising per-customer NRE and engineering intensity for OSATs; favors scale players with engineering depth.
insights.quote: Each customer is different, and there is development work we need to do before we’re ready for verification and high-volume manufacturing.

insights.claim: As substrates become architecture-specific, the qualified supply base can become much smaller than the nominal supply base, and switching suppliers becomes more like qualifying a new manufacturing process than buying an equivalent part.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Incumbent qualified substrate suppliers gain stickiness; new capacity entrants face long qualification lag.
insights.quote: the qualified supply base can become much smaller than the nominal supply base
insights.locator: A supplier with unused factory capacity

insights.claim: Intel Foundry is working with partners to bring silicon-like yield infrastructure into substrate manufacturing, aiming for a 'known good substrate' so no expensive silicon is lost to a nonfunctional substrate.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Inspection, metrology and process control for substrates become a growing spend category.
insights.quote: I’m trying to maintain a known good substrate, so when I attach the silicon, I’m avoiding any loss due to the substrate being not functional
insights.locator: Intel Foundry is working with partners

insights.claim: Because a substrate defect becomes far more costly after high-value logic and HBM are attached, inspection, process control and substrate qualification must move upstream as package costs rise.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Supports demand for upstream substrate inspection/test tools and premium-quality substrates.
insights.locator: That changes the economics of substrate quality

insights.claim: Useful substrate capacity is only the portion qualified for a particular architecture, so aggregate capacity discussions can miss real supply tightness.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Adjust supply/demand models for substrates to qualified-by-architecture capacity.
insights.quote: useful capacity is the portion that has been qualified for that particular architecture
insights.locator: The same logic makes second sourcing

insights.claim: Brewer Science says temporary bonding materials must be redesigned per application around contacted surfaces, adhesion, thermal budget and warpage; even a customer's move from packaging version one to version two can require a material change.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Materials suppliers face fragmentation but also stickier, customized design-ins.
insights.quote: Even if they go from version one of their packaging to version two, we might need to change our material

insights.claim: Temporary-bond process windows are narrow: too little adhesion causes delamination, too high modulus adds stress, and thickness variation degrades fine-pitch RDL uniformity and resolution.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Materials performance directly gates fine-pitch RDL yield.
insights.locator: That process window can be narrow

insights.claim: Moving from wafer to panel-level packaging demands temporary-bond materials with greater thermal and mechanical stability due to non-uniform coatings and higher stress and warpage.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Panel-level transition creates a materials requalification cycle.

insights.claim: Applied Materials found that reducing through-glass-via liner CTE alone did not prevent cracking; a low-CTE, low-modulus liner was needed to address both thermal mismatch and mechanical strain.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Glass-core adoption hinges on unsolved-but-progressing materials engineering like TGV liners.

insights.claim: Applied Materials is pursuing process portability across different glass types because changing glass composition changes stress, seed adhesion and downstream thermal behavior, meaning 'glass' is not one set of conditions.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Glass substrate is not a single standardized platform, raising integration risk and supplier lock-in.
insights.quote: we need to have a solution that works for different types of glass so that the downstream processes don’t change
insights.locator: There are a lot of questions

insights.claim: Lam Research says the industry has not converged on an advanced-packaging substrate paradigm and all approaches require significant additional equipment investment and development.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Equipment vendors carry R&D risk across multiple competing substrate flows before HVM winners are known.
insights.quote: The industry has not yet converged on what the real paradigm will be, and all of these approaches require a lot more investment and development from the equipment industry
insights.locator: The industry has not yet converged

insights.claim: Equipment must be developed and purchased before the eventual production mix is known, since glass-core, organic build-up and panel flows need different handling, via and deposition processes, and finer routing pushes back-end processes toward front-end-like techniques.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Back-end tool intensity rising toward front-end levels expands packaging equipment TAM, but with mix uncertainty.
insights.locator: This creates an awkward capital-equipment problem

insights.claim: AI and HPC packages with large logic and HBM impose the most aggressive substrate requirements (dense routing, many layers, high-speed signaling, hard power delivery) but do not set a universal architecture for other markets.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: AI is the premium substrate driver, but other segments will not follow the same technology path.
insights.locator: AI and HPC are currently pushing

insights.claim: Amkor says co-packaged optics implementations are so new and custom that investing in one architecture may not port to another customer, creating OSAT investment risk.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: CPO capex by OSATs is fragmented; early winners may be those tied to specific customer architectures.
insights.quote: If we invest and say, okay, we’re going to support this particular architecture, it may or may not port over to someone else.

insights.claim: CPO assembly requires new attach, cleaning and inspection capabilities because contamination tolerable in electronics can attenuate light around micro-lens arrays, and some designs need index-matching epoxy while others require a clean air cavity.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: CPO opens new OSAT tool and process categories (optical attach, cleanliness inspection).
insights.locator: The differences reach directly into assembly

insights.claim: Amkor says traditional wire-bond packages remain the workhorse of automotive despite growth in advanced packages for ADAS and centralized compute, driven by cost, reliability and qualification history.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Automotive packaging demand stays in mature, lower-cost formats; don't extrapolate AI substrate trends to auto.
insights.quote: the workhorse of automotive packaging still remains traditional wire-bond packages

themes.theme: Design data gap and no single successor

insights.claim: Synopsys says standardized material technology files for thermal and power behavior of substrates and interposers, integrable into design flows, are still lacking.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Opportunity for EDA vendors and standards bodies; until solved, more physical test vehicles and slower qualification.
insights.quote: Material technology files for thermal and power behavior for interposers and substrates, in a format that can be integrated into the design flow, are still lacking.
insights.locator: There is still a lot of opaqueness

insights.claim: Mitsubishi Chemical Group argues no single process solution fits all and customization requires collaboration among materials suppliers, equipment makers and fabs that operate as proprietary 'black boxes'.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Ecosystem partnerships become a competitive factor for materials suppliers.
insights.quote: There isn’t going to be one solution that fits all. Every process is going to require some customization
insights.locator: There isn't going to be one solution

insights.claim: There will be no single successor substrate: glass brings TGV, adhesion, handling, chipping and cracking problems; organic retains cost and maturity but is challenged by finer routing; bridges and fan-out bring their own yield issues.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Avoid all-in bets on glass-core as the organic replacement; expect a multi-technology substrate market.
insights.quote: The industry is no longer converging on one substrate to rule them all.

insights.claim: Substrate selection is moving toward the beginning of system architecture, as designers must decide what it carries, wiring density, material survivability, supplier yield and modeling before the package is locked.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Substrate suppliers gain earlier design-in leverage and longer customer lock-in.
